config.title: Forms & Validation

intro.title: Forms & Validation
intro.body: In this lesson, you'll build a user registration form with real-time validation. You'll learn how to capture user input, validate it as the user types, and display helpful error messages. The core concept is controlled components, where React state becomes the single source of truth for form data. You'll use TypeScript interfaces to define the shape of your form data and ensure type safety. By the end, you'll have a fully functional form that prevents submission until all validation rules are met.
intro.usecase: Forms with validation are essential in nearly every interactive web application. You'll implement them when building user registration/login screens, checkout processes in e-commerce sites, and data entry interfaces in admin dashboards. For example, when users update their profile information on social media platforms or submit support tickets with required fields, proper validation ensures data quality and prevents errors. As a React developer, you'll frequently create controlled form components with real-time validation feedback to deliver professional user experiences.

objectives: Define TypeScript interfaces to specify the structure and types of form data objects.
Implement controlled form components using useState hooks to manage input values.
Apply event handlers to capture and process user input from form elements.
Utilize form submission handlers to prevent default browser behavior and process form data.
Construct validation functions that check form data against specific rules and criteria.
Execute conditional rendering to display validation error messages based on form state.
Use TypeScript generics with useState to maintain type safety for form state management.
Implement real-time validation by invoking validation logic within change event handlers.
Control form submission flow by conditionally enabling/disabling submit buttons based on validation status.
Store validation results in component state to track and display multiple error conditions.
Compare form field values against validation rules to determine input validity.
Return structured form data from submission handlers for further processing or API calls.

steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.seedCode:
// Import React and useState from 'react' here

// Your component will go below
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have React and useState available for use in your component.
successCriteria: The code must include an import statement that imports React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the useState hook for managing state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'. Check that your import statement includes both.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. You need to import React and useState from the 'react' package using an import statement.

steps.title: Create the main FormComponent
steps.instruction: Create a functional component called FormComponent that returns null for now. Use TypeScript syntax and make sure it's exported.
steps.hint: You can use either a function declaration or arrow function. Remember to export it so it can be imported elsewhere.
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional component named FormComponent is created and exported, returning null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the FormComponent functional component. The component is properly defined and exported, ready for implementation.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there might be something missing. Make sure the component is named exactly 'FormComponent', returns null, and is exported.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component wasn't created correctly. Check that you've defined a function named FormComponent that returns null and is exported.

steps.title: Initialize form state with useState
steps.instruction: Inside your FormComponent, use the useState hook to create a state variable called formData. Initialize it as an empty object {}.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier. The syntax is: const [formData, setFormData] = useState<Record<string, any>>({}); or you can rely on TypeScript's type inference.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component should have a formData state variable initialized as an empty object, ready to store form input values.
successCriteria: Initial value is an empty object {}
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the formData state with an empty object. This gives us a place to store all form input values as the user types.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: Did you name the state variable 'formData'? Is it initialized as an empty object {}?
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Use useState to create a state variable called formData and initialize it with an empty object {}. Remember to call useState inside your component.

steps.title: Initialize validation errors state
steps.instruction: Inside your FormComponent, use useState to create a state variable called errors. Initialize it as an empty object that will store validation error messages.
steps.hint: Add another useState hook call. The state variable should be named errors and its initial value should be an empty object {}.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing an errors state object
const [errors, setErrors] = useState<Record<string, string>>({});
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a new state variable called errors initialized as an empty object, ready to store validation error messages.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the errors state. This empty object will be used to store validation error messages for each form field.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: Did you name the state variable 'errors'? Did you initialize it as an empty object {}?
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to add another useState hook inside FormComponent to create a state variable called errors, initialized as an empty object.

steps.title: Define the handleChange function
steps.instruction: Inside your FormComponent, define a function called handleChange that takes a React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> as a parameter and updates the formData state using the setFormData function.
steps.hint: The function should use the event's target (name and value) to update the corresponding field in the formData state object.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a handleChange function that properly updates the formData state when called with an input change event.
successCriteria:
The handleChange function must:
1. Be defined inside the FormComponent
2. Accept a React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> parameter
3. Extract name and value from event.target
4. Update formData state using setFormData with proper object spreading
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! Your handleChange function correctly updates the formData state by spreading the previous state and updating the specific field based on the input's name attribute.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your handleChange function properly extracts the name and value from the event and updates the formData state correctly. Make sure you're using the setFormData function to update the state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleChange function is missing or incorrect. Remember to define a function that takes a change event, extracts the input's name and value, and updates the formData state using setFormData.

steps.title: Define the validateForm function
steps.instruction: Define a function named validateForm inside your FormComponent that takes no parameters and returns an object with error messages for name and email fields.
steps.hint: Create a function that checks the current formData values and returns an object with error strings. You can use simple validation rules like checking if fields are empty.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a validateForm function that returns an error object based on formData values.
successCriteria: The function should be named validateForm, defined inside the component, and return an object with name and email properties containing error strings.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the validation function. This function will be used later to check form inputs before submission.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your validateForm function returns an object with both name and email error properties. Also ensure it's defined inside the component.
steps.feedbackWrong: The validateForm function isn't defined correctly. Remember to create a function that returns an object with error messages for name and email fields based on formData values.

steps.title: Define the handleSubmit function
steps.instruction: Define a function named handleSubmit that takes a React.FormEvent as parameter, prevents the default form submission behavior, and calls the validateForm function.
steps.hint: Create a function that accepts an event parameter of type React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>, calls e.preventDefault() to stop the page from reloading, and then calls validateForm().
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a handleSubmit function that prevents form submission and triggers validation.
successCriteria: The handleSubmit function should be defined with the correct parameter type, call e.preventDefault(), and call validateForm().
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the handleSubmit function that prevents default form submission and triggers validation.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your handleSubmit function: 1) accepts a React.FormEvent parameter, 2) calls e.preventDefault(), and 3) calls validateForm().
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleSubmit function is missing or incorrect. It should prevent default form behavior and call the validation function.

steps.title: Return a form element
steps.instruction: Inside the return statement of your FormComponent, add a <form> element with an onSubmit handler that calls the handleSubmit function.
steps.hint: The form element should wrap the content you'll add later. Use the onSubmit attribute and pass handleSubmit as the handler.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will now have a form element that will handle form submission when the user submits.
successCriteria: The code should include a <form> element with an onSubmit attribute set to handleSubmit.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the form element with the correct onSubmit handler. This sets up the structure for form submission.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added both the <form> element and the onSubmit attribute with handleSubmit as the handler.
steps.feedbackWrong: The form element or onSubmit handler is missing or incorrect. Check that you've added <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}> inside the return statement.

steps.title: Add a name input field
steps.instruction: Inside the form element, add an input field for the name. Set its type to 'text', name to 'name', value to formData.name, onChange to handleChange, and add a placeholder like 'Enter your name'.
steps.hint: The input should be a controlled component, meaning its value comes from state and changes are handled by the handleChange function.
steps.expectedOutcome: The form will have a text input for the name field that updates the formData state when typed into.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a controlled input for the name field. The input's value is tied to the formData state, and changes are handled by the handleChange function.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added an input, but it might be missing some required attributes. Make sure it has type="text", name="name", value={formData.name}, onChange={handleChange}, and a placeholder.
steps.feedbackWrong: The name input field is not correctly implemented. Check that you've added an input element with the correct attributes to make it a controlled component.

steps.title: Add an email input field
steps.instruction: Add an email input field inside the form element. The input should have: name="email", value={formData.email}, onChange={handleChange}, and placeholder="Enter your email".
steps.hint: Add an <input> element with the specified attributes. Make sure the name matches the key in your formData state.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have an email input field that is controlled by the formData state and updates via the handleChange function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the email input field. It's now properly connected to your formData state and will update when the user types.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added an input field, but check that all required attributes are present: name="email", value={formData.email}, onChange={handleChange}, and placeholder.
steps.feedbackWrong: The email input field is missing or incomplete. Make sure to add an <input> element with all the specified attributes inside the form.

steps.title: Display validation error messages
steps.instruction: Add conditional rendering to display the validation error messages below each input field. For each field, show its error message only when the corresponding error state is not empty.
steps.hint: Use the errors state object to access error messages. You can conditionally render a paragraph element with the error text.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of conditional error rendering {errors.name &&

{errors.name}

}
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will show validation error messages below the corresponding input fields when errors exist.
successCriteria: Error messages are displayed in paragraph elements
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added conditional rendering for validation errors. Users will now see immediate feedback when they submit invalid data.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check if you've added conditional rendering for both name and email errors. Make sure to use the errors state object.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to add conditional rendering that displays error messages when the errors state contains text for each field.

steps.title: Add a submit button
steps.instruction: Inside the form element, add a submit button with the text 'Submit'.
steps.hint: Use the <button> element with type='submit' attribute.
steps.analogousExample:
// Add a submit button inside a form
<form>
  <button type='submit'>Submit</button>
</form>
steps.expectedOutcome: A submit button appears inside the form element.
successCriteria: The code includes a <button> element with type='submit' and the text 'Submit' inside the form element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added a submit button to complete the form.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a button, but make sure it has type='submit' and the text 'Submit'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The submit button is missing or incorrect. Add a <button type='submit'>Submit</button> inside the form.
